slides.headline: Long rides leaving your back stiff?
slides.sub: What clinical Pilates adds to a cyclist's training week.

slides.title: Cycling keeps you in one shape
slides.body: Cycling builds heaps of fitness, but it holds you in the same flexed shape for hours. Pilates gives your hips, spine and shoulders the other directions they rarely get on the bike.

slides.title: Get the glutes sharing the load
slides.body: Many riders lean on their quads and lower back. Bridges, side-lying leg work and reformer footwork help the glutes pitch in, which can make long climbs feel more even.

slides.title: Open up the mid-back
slides.body: Upper back extension and rotation work, like reformer chest expansion or seated twists, can ease that rounded feeling after a long ride and make looking up the road more comfortable.

slides.title: Steady trunk, smoother pedalling
slides.body: Side planks and controlled leg movements train your trunk to stay quiet while your legs work. Many riders notice less rocking on the saddle when they're tired late in a ride.

slides.title: Fitting it into a riding week
slides.body: One or two sessions a week is a good starting point. Slot Pilates in on an easy spin day rather than the day before a big ride, and build up gradually.

slides.headline: Make the bike feel easier
slides.body: Our Pilates team starts with an assessment, then builds a program around your riding, niggles and goals. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Long rides leaving your back stiff? 🚴

Cycling is brilliant for fitness, but it keeps you folded in one position for hours. Clinical Pilates works on everything the bike doesn't: glutes that share the load with your quads, a mid-back that can extend and rotate, and a trunk that stays steady when your legs are tired.

A good starting point is one or two sessions a week, ideally on an easy riding day. Most riders find the program slots in alongside training rather than replacing any of it, and it builds up gradually as you get stronger.

story.headline: Stiff after big rides?
story.body: Swap one easy spin a week for a Pilates session. Your hips and mid-back get the movement the bike doesn't give them.
